children: By Nat Ives, WSJ Leadership Institute

Good morning. If you want ad dollars, you have to put on a show. Rival retail media operators held their first upfront-style pitchfest yesterday to court ad buyers, and the WSJ Leadership Institute's Patrick Coffee was in the room.
Nobody previewed a sexy new reality competition or trotted out former NFL players, but retail media's inaugural Showcase still resembled its TV inspiration in key ways.
Presenters promised peerless value, arguing that their platforms lead directly to consideration and sales, backed by an endless string of data points:
Two-thirds of DoorDash users haven't decided what they want to order when they sign on, and one in five have ordered more than three times in a single day, said Chief Marketing Officer Tim Castree.
PayPal Ads executive Asaf Davidov touted "chief friend officers" who center a social group's spending and are 1.5 times more likely than the average Venmo user to be in the key 18-to-29 demographic.
Lauren Griewski of Chase Media Solutions said JPMorgan Chase transactions account for 6% of the U.S. economy.
Even as they shared a stage to more efficiently pitch advertisers, the networks endeavored to stand apart. Macy's Media Network highlighted its 165-year history with shoppers.
"That relationship is difficult to replicate, and it's what makes our retail media network different from anyone else," said Michael Krans, Macy's vice president of retail media.

These networks are trying to help brands get discovered in a retail world where 80% to 85% of sales still happen in-store, according to Brian Leder, president of media agency Ramp97, who attended the event.

Networks know they must use their data to better anticipate consumer behavior-hence the constant repetition of "consumer intent" at the event-but buyers still have questions around data transparency, Leder noted.
"That's great that we got a 500% [return on ad spend], but if I don't know where that ROAS came from, that's the lack of transparency," he said.
Despite robust attendance at the Showcase, retail media's biggest names-Amazon and Walmart-were nowhere to be found.

"It's well documented that retail media spend is artificially consolidated with a handful of players far beyond their commensurate share of sales," Brian Monahan, senior vice president of Albertsons Media Collective, told the audience in a not-so-subtle reference to those category leaders.
The battle over remaining market share will only intensify.

Albertsons recently hired an in-house creative director to develop branded content, building on "Rico's Tacos," its P&G-produced scripted series that earned buzz at Cannes Lions, Monahan told the WSJ Leadership Institute.
Big Cheese

Goodles built a surprising share of the multibillion-dollar mac-and-cheese business in the U.S. by doing what the incumbents didn't: offering adult flavors with high protein and fiber, standing out with sassy names and colorful boxes, and counting on TikTok and Instagram to spread the word.
Now the quirky challenger brand is officially joining the old guard.
Barilla Group's acquisition of the Santa Cruz, Calif.-based startup sets up the latest test of how a scrappy, social-first company maintains its brand edge after being acquired.
I spoke with WSJ Leadership Institute reporter Megan Graham, who has covered Goodles' rise and had the exclusive on Barilla yesterday, about the deal.

You reported last year that Goodles was taking off partly by being a little bit odd, not a big spender. In addition to those quirky flavor names like Smokey Dokey and Here Comes Truffle, it was selling holographic roller skates and being pen pals with fans. What are the chances that its kind of personalized, unconventional marketing continues under the umbrella of a major, traditional Italian pasta company?

Megan: It sounds like the odds are pretty good on that front. According to CEO Jen Zeszut, the weirdness of Goodles was actually one of its major selling points for Barilla. She said Barilla likes the company "just the way we are" and isn't planning to change a thing-from the zany marketing to the ingredients they use.
But it will be interesting to see what they're able to do with a bigger backing.

Zeszut is also vocal about the idea that her adult-friendly brand can help expand the audience for mac-and-cheese, as opposed to only taking market share from incumbents like Kraft. Why is that so important?

Megan: I think it just speaks to the future of this category overall. A lot of consumers are so much more conscious about what they're eating-carefully examining what they eat, steering clear of mystery chemical ingredients and counting their macros. That poses a big challenge for traditional big food companies that haven't kept up with those concerns.
If Goodles can get people who otherwise wouldn't be eating mac and cheese, it doesn't always have to convert loyalists from other brands, and the category could see bigger growth overall.

I'm probably a good example of this. I'm trying to eat more thoughtfully right now as I get ready for my wedding. And as someone who otherwise regularly houses large quantities of pasta multiple times a week, I might have felt some conflict there. But with some of these higher-protein, higher-fiber options, I'm using substitutes like protein pasta or bone broth rice to keep eating the things I want to eat while being a little more macro-conscious.
The Magic Number

Ford's sales goal for its planned Fathom electric truck in its first year of production, an ambitious target that's only been seen by Tesla in the U.S. The truck is expected to start at around $30,000 and go on sale next year.
